After a vowel other than a/ā, the visarga (रु) appears as r before a voiced sound.

samasa.vigraha: भिन्दिपालाः च असयः च पट्टिशाः च, तैः
samasa.literal: with javelins and swords and paṭṭiśas
samasa.sense: three kinds of weapon: the bhindipāla (a short throwing javelin), the sword and the edged spear

morph.note: kta of an intransitive verb, active in sense and standing for the finite verb: ‘(they) came into being’. The predicate गणाः says what they became.

The numeral शतसहस्र ‘a hundred thousand’ (शत ‘hundred’ + सहस्र ‘thousand’) with the taddhita -शस्, which makes distributive adverbs from numbers and quantities (शतशः ‘by hundreds’, 2.56). It is indeclinable.

mantras.anvaya: ते एव (निःश्वासाः) सद्यः शतसहस्रशः गणाः सम्भूताः। ते (गणाः) परशुभिः भिन्दिपालासिपट्टिशैः (च) युयुधुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The main clause answers the relative clause of 2.52 (यान् … ते एव). The second line begins a new sentence whose participle (नाशयन्तः) runs into 2.54.
mantras.lit: those very (breaths) at once became gaṇas by hundreds of thousands. They fought with axes, with javelins, swords and paṭṭiśas,
mantras.tr: became at once her hosts, hundreds of thousands strong. They fought with axes, javelins, swords and halberds,

comm.t: The Devī’s breath becomes an army. She does not summon allies from outside: her own exhalations take form as gaṇas, hundreds of thousands of them, and go into battle with weapons of their own.

The text itself later states the principle behind this: when Śumbha taunts her for relying on others, the Devī answers that she alone is there, and the powers he saw were hers, returning into her (10.5, एकैवाहं जगत्यत्र). The gaṇas here are an early instance: her helpers are her own power.

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) likewise gives its Goddess an army that is her own power: name 65, भण्डासुरवधोद्युक्तशक्तिसेनासमन्विता, ‘accompanied by an army of śaktis intent on slaying Bhaṇḍāsura’. The idea is shared; the stories are separate.

samasa.sense: the enemy troops — set against the Devī’s own गणाः

samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa (देवीशक्ति)
samasa.literal: made strong by the power of the Devī
samasa.sense: the gaṇas fight with the strength of the one who breathed them out

morph.note: Causative stem नाशय- (√नश् with vṛddhi + णिच्) and the present participle ending -अत् (śatṛ): ‘causing to perish’, i.e. destroying.
Imperfect of the causative वादय- ‘to make speak’, the regular verb for playing an instrument. Causatives take either voice; the ātmanepada ending -अन्त is used here.
Its last member उपबृंहित is the kta of उप + √बृंह् ‘to make great, strengthen’: ‘reinforced’.

mantras.anvaya: (ते गणाः) देवीशक्त्युपबृंहिताः असुरगणान् नाशयन्तः (युयुधुः)। गणाः पटहान् अवादयन्त, तथा अपरे शङ्खान् (अवादयन्त),
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line belongs with 2.53b: participle and qualifier of the fighting gaṇas. The second line starts the list of instruments, which continues in 2.55a.
mantras.lit: destroying the hosts of the asuras, strengthened by the Devī’s power. (Some) gaṇas sounded war-drums, and likewise others conches,
mantras.tr: destroying the asura hosts, made mighty by the Goddess’s power. Some of the hosts beat the war-drums, others blew the conches,
mantras.tr_note: ‘Beat’ and ‘blew’ render the one verb अवादयन्त ‘sounded’ for each instrument.

comm.t: The gaṇas both fight and make music. Their strength is not their own: it is the Devī’s power (देवीशक्ति) that swells them. Drums and conches are the sounds of an army sure of victory.
A modern reading: the same beings destroy and celebrate in one breath. The text does not separate the battle from the festival — 2.55 will call it a ‘great festival of war’.

samasa.type: karmadhāraya (a metaphor, rūpaka: the battle is identified with a festival) containing a karmadhāraya (महोत्सव)
samasa.literal: in the battle that was a great festival
samasa.sense: the war, celebrated with drums and conches, is a festival for the Devī’s side
samasa.alt: Also read as a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, युद्धस्य महोत्सवः ‘the great festival of battle’; the identifying karmadhāraya fits the drums and conches of 2.54–55.

samasa.sense: the trident, the gift of Śiva (2.20)

morph.note: Locative singular of the pronoun तद् (masculine/neuter), with the pronominal ending -स्मिन्.

mantras.anvaya: अन्ये च तथा एव तस्मिन् युद्धमहोत्सवे मृदङ्गान् (अवादयन्त)। ततः देवी त्रिशूलेन गदया शक्तिवृष्टिभिः —
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line closes the sentence of 2.54b (the verb अवादयन्त is carried over). The second line opens a new sentence whose verb, निजघान, is in 2.56.
mantras.lit: and others, just so, (sounded) mṛdaṅgas in that great festival of battle. Then the Devī, with the trident, with the mace, with showers of spears —
mantras.tr: and others the mṛdaṅga drums, in that great festival of war. Then the Goddess, with trident and mace and showers of spears,

comm.t: The orchestra is completed — war-drums, conches, mṛdaṅgas — and the battle is named a ‘great festival’. Then the Devī herself takes up her weapons: the trident, the mace and the spear-showers begin the list that runs into 2.56.
Several of these weapons are the gods’ gifts of 2.20–24: Śiva’s trident, Agni’s śakti, and the sword (2.56) given by Kāla. The armed form the gods made is now at work.

samasa.sense: with the sword and her other weapons
the asura champions (महत् takes the form महा- as the first member of a karmadhāraya)

samasa.literal: stupefied by the sound of the bell
samasa.sense: dazed by the ringing of the bell Indra gave her (2.22)

morph.note: Perfect of √हन्: in the reduplicated form the h appears as j in the reduplicating syllable and as gh in the root (ज-घान), with vṛddhi of the root vowel in the 3rd singular.
Periphrastic perfect: the causative stem पातय- + -आम् + the perfect of √अस् (आस). Causatives form their perfect only this way.

mantras.anvaya: (ततः देवी त्रिशूलेन गदया शक्तिवृष्टिभिः) खड्गादिभिः च शतशः महासुरान् निजघान। घण्टास्वनविमोहितान् अन्यान् च एव पातयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the sentence of 2.55b with its object and verb. The second adds a parallel clause with the same subject.
mantras.lit: and with the sword and the rest, struck down the great asuras by hundreds; and she felled others, stupefied by the sound of the bell.
mantras.tr: with sword and every other weapon, struck down the great asuras by the hundred; and others, dazed by the ringing of her bell, she brought to the ground.

comm.t: The Devī’s own slaughter begins. Even her bell is a weapon: its sound stupefies the asuras before they are felled.

The bell is Indra’s gift, taken from Airāvata (2.22). It returns in the gods’ hymn of the eleventh chapter, which asks that the bell that fills the world with its sound and destroys the daityas’ might protect them from sin, as one guards one’s children (11.27).

samasa.literal: by the fallings of the sword

morph.note: Absolutive of √बन्ध्: the nasal drops (बध्), and dh + t → ddh (बद्ध्वा). The binding precedes the dragging.
A causative form (कर्षय-) with the meaning of the simple verb ‘dragged’; the causative suffix here adds no ‘make someone do’. The simple imperfect would be अकर्षत्.
Numeral adverb with -धा: द्विधा ‘in two (parts)’, here with कृताः ‘were cut in two’.

mantras.anvaya: अन्यान् च असुरान् पाशेन बद्ध्वा भुवि अकर्षयत्। केचित् तीक्ष्णैः खड्गपातैः द्विधा कृताः। तथा अपरे —
mantras.anvaya_en: First line: absolutive + finite verb with the Devī as subject. Second: a passive participle as verb with an instrumental of means. अपरे opens the sentence completed in 2.58.
mantras.lit: And binding other asuras with the noose, she dragged (them) on the ground. Some were made in two by sharp sword-strokes; likewise others —
mantras.tr: Others she bound with her noose and dragged along the ground. Some were cut in two by the keen strokes of her sword; and others —
mantras.tr_note: भुवि may also go with बद्ध्वा (‘bound on the ground’); the readable version joins it to the dragging.

comm.t: Each weapon has its own work: the noose binds and drags, the sword cuts in two. The verse begins the catalogue of the asuras’ deaths that runs to 2.64.
The noose is Varuṇa’s gift (2.23). In iconography the pāśa is the binding power that the Goddess holds over those who oppose her.
